newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria PM hopes to reach IMF deal next week.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria PM hopes to reach IMF deal next week.

text.p: Bulgaria's interim prime minister said on Wednesday he hoped for a deal next week with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), whose negotiators want pledges that a new government will stick to any accord that is reached.
Interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski said he hoped his cabinet and the IMF would soon resolve differences over a reform and funding arrangement.

"The talks have advanced well but there are a few problems before we reach a final agreement...I believe early next week we will have a final understanding of where we stand. These talks cannot last forever," Sofianski told reporters.

Earlier on Wednesday IMF Europe One department director Michael Deppler said he needed assurances that the new government to take office after April 19 general elections would be committed to the reform programme currently being hammered out.

Speaking after a meeting with Deppler, Sofianski said they had agreed on most issues related to the implementation of a fixed exchange rate system, called a currency board, to help stabilise the crumbling economy and repay foreign debts.
"We have agreed on most issues, the structural reform, the budget and the principles of the currency board. Differences remain in the bank stabilisation policies," said Sofianski.

The currency board system would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing the printing of money.

"We prefer to stabilise our banks before the introduction of the currency board system, which will make the system more sustainable. The IMF recommends to do it under the currency board," said Sofianski.
The IMF recommends to sell four ailing banks by year-end and seek reputable foreign institutions to manage two other big ailing state banks, one banker said.
But local bankers would like loans to re-capitalise the ailing banks and then offer them to investors.

IMF recommendations are based on a seven-year history of uncontrolled lending and mismangement of Bulgarian banks that has led to placing one-third of them in receivership, said the banker, who declined to be named.
Deppler, who plans to stay until the end of this week, said there were no practical obstacles in reaching a funding arrangement with the interim cabinet.
The programme will also contain legal amendments to bank laws designed jointly with the IMF to enable the introduction of a currency board in June.
Deppler said he planned to seek guarantees of continuity in meetings with the main political parties. -- Sofia Newsroom 3592 981 4145
